note.explanation: A reversible reaction at equilibrium can be disturbed by changing the amounts of reactants or products, the temperature, or—when gases are involved—the pressure. The reaction then shifts in a direction that helps establish equilibrium again. A catalyst makes equilibrium happen sooner but does not change the equilibrium position.
examples: Adding N₂ to N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) makes the reaction move forward and form more NH₃.
Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas. For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), that is the forward side.
note.checkAnswer: The forward and backward reaction rates increase equally; the catalyst makes equilibrium take less time to reach.
note.simple: If you disturb an equilibrium, the reaction shifts to help restore it. A catalyst only helps it get there faster.
note.checkQuestion: What does a catalyst do to a reversible reaction at equilibrium?
note.title: Changing conditions at equilibrium
steps: Identify what changed: the amount of a substance, temperature, or pressure.
For a changed amount, note whether a reactant or product was added or removed.
For temperature, use whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
For pressure, compare the total moles of gaseous substances on both sides.
Remember that a catalyst speeds up both directions and reduces the time to reach equilibrium.
note.answer: A catalyst increases the rates of both forward and backward reactions, so equilibrium is reached in less time.

options: More NH₃ will form.
The reaction will shift backward and form more N₂ and H₂.
The equilibrium position will not change.
The reaction will stop.
mcqs.stem: At equilibrium, more N₂ is added to N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). What happens as the system restores equilibrium?
rationales: Adding a reactant makes the reaction use it by moving forward and forming more ammonia.
The backward shift would produce more of the N₂ that was already added, rather than use it.
Adding a reacting species disturbs the equilibrium and changes the concentrations.
A reversible reaction continues in both directions at equilibrium; it does not stop.

options: The forward reaction is favoured.
The backward reaction is favoured.
There is no effect because there are gases on both sides.
The reaction stops at once.
mcqs.stem: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), which direction is favoured when pressure is increased?
rationales: There are fewer moles of gas on the product side, so increased pressure favours the forward direction.
The backward direction has more gaseous moles, so it is not favoured by increased pressure.
Pressure can affect a gaseous equilibrium when the numbers of gaseous moles differ across the reaction.
Changing pressure disturbs the equilibrium; it does not make the reaction stop.

options: The forward direction.
The backward direction.
Neither direction, because temperature never affects equilibrium.
Both directions stop.
mcqs.stem: The forward formation of ammonia is exothermic. What direction is favoured when the temperature is increased?
rationales: Increasing temperature does not favour the exothermic forward direction in this reaction.
The reverse direction is endothermic, so increasing temperature favours the backward direction.
Temperature can disturb equilibrium, and this section describes its effect on ammonia formation.
A temperature change shifts the equilibrium; it does not stop both reactions.

options: It increases only the forward reaction rate.
It increases only the backward reaction rate.
It increases both reaction rates and reduces the time taken to reach equilibrium.
It changes the equilibrium concentrations but not the reaction rates.
mcqs.stem: What is the effect of adding a catalyst to a reversible reaction?
rationales: A catalyst increases the rates of both directions, not only the forward reaction.
A catalyst increases the rates of both directions, not only the backward reaction.
A catalyst speeds up both reactions, so the system reaches equilibrium sooner.
A catalyst affects reaction rates; it does not change the equilibrium concentrations.

options: Equilibrium shifts to the side with fewer moles of gas.
Equilibrium shifts to the side with more moles of gas.
Pressure always favours the reactants.
Pressure has the same effect even when the gas-mole numbers are equal.
mcqs.stem: When can a pressure change disturb a gaseous equilibrium, and which side does increased pressure favour?
rationales: When gaseous mole numbers differ, increased pressure favours the side with fewer gaseous moles.
Increased pressure favours the side with fewer, not more, gaseous moles.
Pressure does not always favour reactants; the direction depends on gaseous mole numbers on both sides.
If the gaseous mole numbers are equal on both sides, a pressure change does not shift the equilibrium position.

options: Remove some reactant.
Add more of the product.
Remove product as it forms.
Add a catalyst and expect a larger equilibrium yield.
mcqs.stem: Which change can help force a reversible reaction towards completion?
rationales: Removing reactant does not drive the reaction towards making more product.
Adding product does not help drive the reaction forward.
Removing product as it forms disturbs equilibrium and can drive the reaction towards further product formation.
A catalyst helps equilibrium be reached sooner but does not increase the equilibrium yield.

options: The concentration of every species stays constant.
All forward and backward reactions stop.
The reactants are completely used up.
Only the product concentration keeps increasing.
mcqs.stem: What happens to the concentrations when an equilibrium system is left undisturbed?
rationales: At equilibrium, the concentrations of all participating species remain constant.
Equilibrium is dynamic: forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates.
A reversible reaction does not necessarily use up all its reactants at equilibrium.
At equilibrium, product concentrations do not keep increasing; they remain constant.

options: The system shifts towards forming more PCl₅.
The system shifts towards forming more PCl₃ and Cl₂.
The equilibrium position does not change because the product gases are removed.
Both reaction directions stop.
mcqs.stem: For PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g), what happens if some Cl₂ is added to the equilibrium mixture?
rationales: The added product is not used by shifting towards more PCl₅; the system shifts to consume added Cl₂.
The backward reaction consumes some of the added Cl₂ and forms more PCl₅, so this option is incorrect as phrased? Wait: adding product favours backward direction, not forward.

written.text: How is dynamic equilibrium different from the static equilibrium?
written.finalAnswer: At dynamic equilibrium, forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates; in static equilibrium, there is no ongoing change or movement.

rubric.why: This states the defining feature of dynamic equilibrium.
rubric.description: Dynamic reactions continue at equal rates.
rubric.how: State that both forward and reverse reactions continue and have equal rates.

rubric.why: The comparison distinguishes dynamic equilibrium from a static state.
rubric.description: Static equilibrium has no ongoing change or movement.
rubric.how: Contrast continued reaction with no ongoing movement or change.

modelAnswer: At dynamic equilibrium, the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates.
At static equilibrium, there is no ongoing change or movement.

written.text: How can you get the maximum yield in a reversible reaction?
written.finalAnswer: Use conditions that favour the product side and withdraw one or more products from the reaction mixture as soon as they are formed.

rubric.why: Favouring the product side increases the amount of product formed.
rubric.description: Use conditions that favour the product side.
rubric.how: State that conditions should drive the equilibrium in the forward direction.

rubric.why: Removing product as it forms can force the reaction further towards completion.
rubric.description: Withdraw product from the reaction mixture as it forms.
rubric.how: State that one or more products should be removed as soon as they are formed.

modelAnswer: Use conditions that favour the product side.
Withdraw one or more products from the reaction mixture as soon as they are formed.

written.text: How can you decrease the time to attain the position of equilibrium in a reversible reaction?
written.finalAnswer: Add a catalyst; it increases the rates of both the forward and backward reactions, decreasing the time taken to attain equilibrium.

rubric.why: The catalyst is the method the textbook gives for reaching equilibrium sooner.
rubric.description: Add a catalyst.
rubric.how: Name a catalyst as the method.

rubric.why: Explaining its effect on both directions shows why equilibrium is reached sooner.
rubric.description: It increases both reaction rates and reduces the time taken.
rubric.how: State that both forward and backward rates increase, so equilibrium is reached sooner.

modelAnswer: Add a catalyst to the reversible reaction.
It increases the rates of both forward and backward reactions, so the time taken to attain equilibrium decreases.

written.text:
What is the effect of increasing pressure on the following reaction at equilibrium?

N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)
written.finalAnswer: There is no effect on the equilibrium position because the number of moles of gaseous reactants and products is equal.

rubric.why: This gives the effect of pressure on the stated equilibrium.
rubric.description: The equilibrium position does not shift.
rubric.how: State that increasing pressure has no effect on the equilibrium position.

rubric.why: The equal gaseous mole numbers explain why pressure does not shift the equilibrium.
rubric.description: There are two gaseous moles on each side.
rubric.how: Compare the two moles of gaseous reactants with the two moles of gaseous products.

modelAnswer: Reactant side: 1 mole N₂ + 1 mole O₂ = 2 moles of gas.
Product side: 2 moles of NO gas.
The number of gaseous moles is equal on both sides, so increasing pressure has no effect on the equilibrium position.

written.text:
How can you drive the reversible reaction at equilibrium?

(a) in the forward direction
(b) in the backward direction
written.finalAnswer: Drive it forward by adding reactants or withdrawing products. Drive it backward by adding products or withdrawing reactants.

rubric.why: Adding reactants can drive the reaction towards products.
rubric.description: Forward: add reactants.
rubric.how: Give adding reactants as one way to drive the reaction forward.

rubric.why: Removing products can drive the reaction towards further product formation.
rubric.description: Forward: withdraw products.
rubric.how: Give withdrawing products as another way to drive the reaction forward.

rubric.why: Adding products can drive the reaction towards reactants.
rubric.description: Backward: add products.
rubric.how: Give adding products as one way to drive the reaction backward.

rubric.why: Removing reactants can drive the reaction towards the reactant side.
rubric.description: Backward: withdraw reactants.
rubric.how: Give withdrawing reactants as another way to drive the reaction backward.

modelAnswer: (a) Add reactants or withdraw products to drive the reaction in the forward direction.
(b) Add products or withdraw reactants to drive the reaction in the backward direction.

written.text: Describe the effect of a catalyst on the reversible reaction.
written.finalAnswer: A catalyst increases the rates of both forward and backward reactions. It decreases the time taken to attain equilibrium but does not change the equilibrium position.

rubric.why: A catalyst increases the rate of the forward reaction.
rubric.description: The forward reaction becomes faster.
rubric.how: State that the forward reaction rate increases.

rubric.why: A catalyst also increases the rate of the backward reaction.
rubric.description: The backward reaction becomes faster.
rubric.how: State that the backward reaction rate increases too.

rubric.why: The faster reactions allow equilibrium to be attained sooner.
rubric.description: It decreases the time taken to reach equilibrium.
rubric.how: Explain that equilibrium is attained in less time.

rubric.why: This distinguishes the rate effect from a change in equilibrium position.
rubric.description: It does not change the equilibrium position.
rubric.how: State that the catalyst changes the time, not the equilibrium position.

modelAnswer: A catalyst increases the rates of both forward and backward reactions.
It decreases the time taken to attain equilibrium.
It does not change the equilibrium position.

written.text: How can a reversible reaction be forced to go to completion?
written.finalAnswer: Withdraw one or all of the products from the reaction mixture as soon as they are formed.

rubric.why: Removing products is the method that drives the reversible reaction towards completion.
rubric.description: Withdraw one or all products.
rubric.how: State that product or products must be withdrawn from the mixture.

rubric.why: Removing products as they form prevents them from building up in the mixture.
rubric.description: Remove products as soon as they are formed.
rubric.how: Include that withdrawal should happen as soon as the product is formed.

modelAnswer: Withdraw one or all of the products from the reaction mixture.
Remove them as soon as they are formed.

written.text: How does change in temperature affect the reaction at equilibrium?
written.finalAnswer: Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction, while decreasing temperature favours the exothermic direction. For ammonia formation, the forward reaction is exothermic, so increasing temperature favours the backward direction and decreasing temperature favours the forward direction.

rubric.why: This gives the general effect of increasing temperature.
rubric.description: Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction.
rubric.how: State that the endothermic direction is favoured when temperature increases.

rubric.why: This gives the general effect of decreasing temperature.
rubric.description: Decreasing temperature favours the exothermic direction.
rubric.how: State that the exothermic direction is favoured when temperature decreases.

rubric.why: Identifying the forward reaction as exothermic applies the rule to the textbook example.
rubric.description: Ammonia formation is exothermic in the forward direction.
rubric.how: Identify the forward direction of ammonia formation as exothermic.

rubric.why: This correctly predicts the direction of the ammonia equilibrium after heating.
rubric.description: Increasing temperature drives ammonia equilibrium backward.
rubric.how: State that heating favours the reactant side for ammonia formation.

rubric.why: This correctly predicts the direction of the ammonia equilibrium after cooling.
rubric.description: Decreasing temperature drives ammonia equilibrium forward.
rubric.how: State that cooling favours ammonia formation.

modelAnswer: Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction, and decreasing temperature favours the exothermic direction.
The forward formation of ammonia is exothermic.
Increasing temperature drives the ammonia equilibrium in the backward direction, towards the reactants.
Decreasing temperature drives it in the forward direction, towards ammonia.

written.text: Synthesis of ammonia gas is very important industrially because it is used in the preparation of urea fertilizer. Explain the conditions you will use to get the maximum yield of ammonia.
written.finalAnswer: Use high pressure because the forward reaction produces fewer moles of gas. Use a lower temperature because ammonia formation is exothermic. Remove or liquefy ammonia as it forms to drive the reaction forward. A catalyst makes equilibrium arrive sooner but does not increase the equilibrium yield.

rubric.why: High pressure favours the side with fewer gaseous moles, which is the ammonia side.
rubric.description: Use high pressure.
rubric.how: Explain that the forward reaction makes fewer moles of gas, so high pressure favours ammonia.

rubric.why: Cooling favours the exothermic forward reaction described in the section.
rubric.description: Use lower temperature to favour the exothermic forward direction.
rubric.how: Link lower temperature to increased ammonia formation.

rubric.why: Removing product drives the reaction towards further product formation.
rubric.description: Withdraw or liquefy ammonia as it forms.
rubric.how: State that ammonia is removed or liquefied as it forms.

rubric.why: A catalyst helps reach equilibrium sooner, which is useful in production.
rubric.description: Use a catalyst to reduce the time to equilibrium.
rubric.how: State its rate or time benefit without claiming that it changes equilibrium yield.

rubric.why: This correctly distinguishes a catalyst's effect on reaction time from its effect on yield.
rubric.description: A catalyst does not change the equilibrium position or yield.
rubric.how: Clarify that a catalyst speeds attainment but does not raise the equilibrium yield.

modelAnswer: Use high pressure because 4 moles of reacting gases form 2 moles of product gas, so pressure favours the forward direction.
Use a lower temperature because formation of ammonia is exothermic in the forward direction.
Remove or liquefy ammonia as it forms to drive the reaction towards further ammonia production.
Use a catalyst to increase the rates of both reactions and reduce the time taken to reach equilibrium; it does not change the equilibrium yield.

examTips: Expect short questions asking what happens when a reactant or product is added or withdrawn.
For pressure questions, count only gaseous moles on each side; increased pressure favours the side with fewer gaseous moles.
For temperature questions, identify which direction is exothermic or endothermic before stating the shift.
For a catalyst question, earn marks by saying it increases both forward and backward rates and reduces the time to reach equilibrium.
In longer answers, state the change, explain the direction of shift, and link it to the new equilibrium or product yield.

hints: Compression means the pressure is increased.
Count the gaseous moles on each side and use the side with fewer moles.
yourTurn.question: What will happen if the gas mixture is compressed?
solution: For PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g), there is 1 mole of gas on the left and 2 moles of gas on the right.
The equilibrium shifts to the side with fewer moles of gas.
Therefore, the equilibrium shifts backward and more PCl₅ is formed.
yourTurn.answer: The equilibrium shifts backward, towards PCl₅, because that side has fewer moles of gas.

hints: Cl₂ is a product in this equation.
The reaction shifts in the direction that uses up some of the added product.
yourTurn.question: What will happen if we add Cl₂ gas to the equilibrium mixture?
solution: Cl₂ is a product in PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g).
Adding Cl₂ disturbs the equilibrium by increasing the product concentration.
The reaction shifts backward to use some of the added Cl₂.
More PCl₅ is formed as the system reaches a new equilibrium.
yourTurn.answer: The equilibrium shifts backward and more PCl₅ is formed.

steps.why: This is the reversible reaction shown in the section and identifies the reacting substances.
Adding nitrogen increases its concentration and disturbs the equilibrium.
steps.text: At equilibrium, if we add more N₂ gas in the mixture, its concentration will increase.

steps.why: The reaction uses the added reactant by proceeding in the forward direction.
steps.text: To restore the equilibrium state again, nitrogen will react with hydrogen to produce more ammonia.

steps.why: The concentrations become constant again when the new equilibrium is reached.
steps.text: This change will go on until a new state of equilibrium is reached at which the concentrations of all the species will again become constant.

example.question: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), what happens when more N₂ gas is added to the mixture at equilibrium?
example.answer: The reaction shifts forward, and more ammonia is produced until a new equilibrium is reached.

explain.title: A reversible system can be disturbed
explain.body: Adding or withdrawing reactants or products changes their concentrations. The reaction shifts and, after a time, reaches a new equilibrium where the concentrations are constant again.

explain.title: Temperature changes the direction favoured
explain.body: The section states: “The formation of ammonia is exothermic in the forward direction and hence this reaction will be endothermic in the reverse direction.” Increasing temperature drives ammonia formation backward; decreasing temperature drives it forward.

explain.title: Pressure matters for some gas reactions
explain.body: A pressure change disturbs a gaseous equilibrium when the total gaseous mole numbers differ on the two sides. Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gaseous moles.

explain.title: A catalyst speeds up both directions
explain.body: The section states: “A catalyst increases both the rates of forward and back reactions of a reversible reaction.” It decreases the time taken to attain equilibrium.

mistakes: Saying that a catalyst moves equilibrium towards products; it speeds up both directions and does not change the equilibrium position.
Forgetting to count gaseous moles on both sides before predicting the effect of pressure.
Treating increased temperature as always favouring the forward reaction; use the exothermic or endothermic direction given.
Saying the reaction stops at equilibrium; the forward and backward reactions continue.
Claiming that all reversible reactions go to completion without withdrawing products.
